author: Bill Maurer
title: Shares of Tesla ( TSLA ) tumbled in Thursday afternoon tradi
text:
Shares of Tesla ( TSLA ) tumbled in Thursday afternoon trading after a glaring report from CNBC detailed trouble at the company's Gigafactory that continued to hold back Model 3 production plans. While some issues might not be a surprise given multiple delays that Tesla has already announced, it further cements the notion that the company's window to capture the mass market EV space is closing rather fast.

( Source: Yahoo Finance )
According to the article, Tesla was making some of the batteries by hand and borrowing scores of workers from Panasonic to help with manual assembly. This was happening as late as mid-December, when the company still hadn't gotten to a consistent production rate of 1,000 units per week. Additionally, one insider detailed that with no redundancy, every time one process shuts down the whole line shuts down. With things not operating at full capacity, this is not a welcome sign.
CNBC also raised some issues about battery quality, noting that putting the battery modules together by hand could lead to a variety of problems, and that insiders' reports to management were slapped down. A number of key issues detailed in the article seem to confirm the Daily Kanban article from October 2017 that many Tesla supporters were quick to strike down like a lot of excess waste which can explain why margins have been so poor.
On the flip side, we have pro-Tesla sites like Electrek citing examples of reservations opening up for Model 3 holders not in California or ones placed after the first day . Electrek also seems to dispute the CNBC article, noting that mid-December was before Tesla started to figure out the issues, and that evidence of more reservation e-mails means production is getting better. Analyst Trip Chowdhry even went so far as calling the report "junk," noting that employee activity level at Tesla on Saturday was 10 times as much as Apple ( AAPL ), Facebook ( FB ), Oracle ( ORCL ), and Cisco ( CSCO ). I'm not sure what any of those names have to do with vehicle manufacturing, and remember that Chowdhry once said Tesla would be producing 800 Model Xs a week in December 2015, a rate that the company didn't get to for several more quarters. 
The Tesla forums are a good place to find information regarding many of the company's vehicles and its customers, and there was a very interesting post earlier this week. The poster went to the showroom outside of Miami, Florida, that was showcasing the Model 3, looking to get more information as well as see the vehicle. Despite being very skeptical, the poster said that a showroom employee noted the following information (bold is mine):
The lady at the front of the line overheard my conversation and tried to assure me it wouldn't be that long and that they were ramping up production. I spouted off how they weren't even supposed to get up to 5,000 per week until the year is half over. She gave me a knowing look and said that they're getting the numbers from corporate and that they're up. I raised my eyebrows and gave her a crap look. She gave me the same look again. I gave her a disgusted crap look with an arm fold. Then, she glanced sideways looked back at me and said more quietly " 4,000 per week right now ."
Considering that Tesla wasn't even at 1,000 units per week at the end of December, it seems highly skeptical that they have gotten to 4,000 in just a couple of weeks. Obviously, management wants to put on a good face to keep people from canceling their deposits, but I hope either management or employees aren't handing out completely false information. If we look at Elon Musk's Twitter account , the last reference of the Model 3 is a retweet from mid-December, not even his tweet, and the last time he mentioned anything close to the Model 3 was the "camped on the roof" tweet in late October when the Gigafactory was having lots of problems. If things were doing so much better, wouldn't the CEO be tweeting up a storm like he does with everything else he is involved in?
At the moment, I'm more inclined to believe the CNBC article and the notion that problems are still plaguing Model 3 production. Why? Well, we still haven't learned of the standard battery going into production, which is when volumes are likely to jump because this model is so much cheaper and that's where most consumers are interested. Tesla reports earnings on February 7th, so we'll find out the truth then, but we'll get a potential preview next week when InsideEvs gives its January sales estimate for all Tesla models.
